headline: Saying “excuse me for disturbing you” is, word by word, an honorific, a “nuisance”, and “do”.
An amateur is a “plain person” — and the “person” part is a form of 人 that never stands on its own.
“By oneself” began as “body” plus a possessive plus “quality”, and its ず is a softened つ.
The bentō was probably a “face tub” — and the 弁 was picked to avoid another character's meaning.
“Flashy” may come from a lively “breaking melody” on the shamisen — the 派 is only ateji.
Asia comes through Dutch — and the kanji for it came from Chinese.
Coffee came by way of Dutch, with English leaning on it, from an Arabic word — and it has two twins.
A girl is a “female child” — with a second, rarer name built on another word for “woman”.
A workplace mixes a Chinese-derived “job” with a native-sounding “place” — a clue that it was coined in Japan.
The crescent moon is the “third-day moon”: a moon named for the third day of a lunar month.
Whereabouts is “the direction one goes” — and its last syllable is a worn-down he.
A museum is a “building of wide learning”.
A lost child is a “wandering child” — with the middle syllable worn away.
Sleeping in is, word for word, a “sleeping boy”.
“Gram” was once ガラム — like ガラス and グラス, before it settled.
“Unskilled” may be “at the edge” of what you can do.
Gymnastics got its name in the early Meiji school reforms, when physical education joined the curriculum.
Fur is “hair-skin” — with a Chinese-derived twin of the same spelling attested centuries earlier.
A razor is “hair-shaver” — and the kanji came ready-made from Chinese.
“Citizen” came from Chinese — but a native “country” and “people” compound hides behind the same spelling.
A crowd is “people” who are “full”.
Politely “your home” mixes a native honorific with a Chinese-derived word for “home”.
A bus, a bath and a bass all hide in one two-syllable word.
Hiragana is “smooth kana”, with かな voiced to がな.
A policy is literally a “direction needle” — another name for a magnetic needle.
To stand out is, quite literally, for the “eye” to “stand”.
A humble “I hear you” is “receive” plus “be granted”.
A full name is “surname” plus “given name”, and Japanese has two Chinese readings for it.
“Futile” is probably kin to “empty” — and its kanji are just stand-ins.
An eraser is a native “erasing” stuck to a Dutch-derived “rubber”.
